planting.note: Divide and transplant congested clumps in early spring while dormant, since the wiry black rhizomes resent disturbance once actively growing.

directions: Dahurian bugbane thrives in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in dappled to full shade, echoing the cool woodland-margin habitat of its native Siberia, Mongolia, and northeastern China. Divide congested clumps in early spring, since the wiry black rhizomes resent disturbance once established and take a full season to recover. Tall branching racemes of small white flowers rise well above the ternately compound foliage in late summer, drawing late-season pollinators to an otherwise quiet shade border. This is one of the traditional source plants for the TCM root drug sheng ma, so gardeners growing it for that purpose should let clumps mature several years before any harvest.

planting.note: Site divisions in cool, sheltered shade in early spring, giving the coarse foliage room to expand without wind exposure.

directions: Heracleifolia bugbane carries broad, deeply lobed leaves that echo cow parsnip (Heracleum), giving this coarse-textured woodland species presence even before its late-summer flower spikes appear. Give it cool, evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from drying wind that can scorch the large leaflets. Wiry branched racemes of small white flowers stand well above the foliage and are followed by dry follicles rather than showy berries. Like its relative A. dahurica, the rhizome is one of the traditional source roots for the TCM drug sheng ma, though garden plants are grown primarily for their bold foliage and late bloom.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into leaf-litter-mulched shade beds in spring; small clumps establish faster than the larger Actaea species.

directions: Asian baneberry is a compact woodland species from Japan, Korea, and northeastern China, forming a modest clump of ternately divided leaves topped by a short raceme of small white flowers in late spring. Unlike the familiar white-berried A. pachypoda or red-berried A. rubra, this species ripens glossy black berries in summer, a useful identification feature though all Actaea berries remain toxic if eaten. Plant divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in full to partial shade, where leaf litter mulch will mimic its native forest floor. Its smaller stature suits intimate shade plantings and rock-garden woodland edges better than the towering A. simplex cultivars.
